problem.heading:
What changed—and
what should we inspect?
problem.intro: A movement signal becomes more useful when the team can relate it to loading, weather, drainage and site work.

cards.title: Movement without a clear cause
cards.body: Foundation movement, connection changes and nearby works can affect a structure differently. Separate local rotation, target displacement and vibration instead of treating one reading as the whole condition.

cards.title: Several influences at once
cards.body: Wind, traffic and thermal changes affect structural readings. Blocked drainage or water entering a cable chamber creates a separate maintenance task. Monitor both where the asset’s exposure warrants it.

cards.title: Limited access and dispersed assets
cards.body: An asset-linked history helps engineers prioritise visits, prepare the right checks and compare observations across the same structure. Keep the inspection outcome with the monitored point.

problem.takeaway: Choose the quantities that answer the asset’s engineering question, then connect each exception to an agreed review.

focus.eyebrow: A MEASUREMENT PLAN FOR THE WHOLE ASSET
focus.heading:
Observe the behaviour.
Keep the context.
focus.intro: Use a common asset reference while giving each quantity its own mounting, acquisition and review requirements.

stages.title: Define the concern
stages.body: Identify rotation, vibration, separation or water accumulation—and the decision each measurement will support.

stages.title: Specify the channels
stages.body: Match range, frequency response, acquisition timing and installation to the physical behaviour. Dynamic vibration needs its own specification.

stages.title: Align the evidence
stages.body: Record axes, datums and timestamps. Compare selected readings with temperature, operating events and inspection history.

stages.title: Assign the response
stages.body: Agree engineering review limits, site access and escalation responsibilities before enabling notifications.

focus.note: A monitoring system supports engineering assessment; it does not independently certify capacity, diagnose damage or replace inspection.
focus.detailTitle: Why is structural vibration a separate selection task?
focus.detail: Hitelecom’s published vibration family is designed for machinery, with a 10–5,000 Hz measurement range and vibration velocity RMS output. Large civil structures may require lower-frequency response, different sensitivity, synchronisation or waveform capture. Specify those requirements with the structural engineer before choosing an instrument or promising an analysis. Likewise, target-distance changes require a stable reference; settlement, crack width and strain call for their own suitable measurement methods.

measurements.heading:
Every quantity answers
a different question.
measurements.intro: Specify a measurement for the decision—not simply another sensor for the dashboard.

rows.measure: Local tilt against the installed reference
rows.decision: Which element shows a sustained change in orientation?
rows.selection: Axes, mount rigidity, uncertainty and baseline

rows.decision: How does the observed response change with traffic or works?
rows.selection: Low-frequency response, sensitivity, timing and analysis needs

rows.measure: Radar distance along one measuring axis
rows.decision: Has separation to the stable reference changed?
rows.selection: Target geometry, reference stability and site validation

rows.decision: Does the movement correlate with thermal conditions?
rows.selection: Representative probe location and aligned timestamps

rows.measure: Level at a named pit, channel or underpass
rows.decision: Does rising water require an operational inspection?
rows.selection: Datum, exposure, expected rate of rise and reporting

rows.measure: Water contact at a selected leak-sensing point
rows.decision: Is unwanted water reaching an electrical or communications asset?
rows.selection: Probe placement, wet-test coverage, drainage route and response time

rows.measure: Specialist crack-width, strain or settlement measurement
rows.decision: Which physical change needs independent quantification?
rows.selection: Engineer-selected instrument, reference, acquisition and analysis scope

measurements.boundary: Crack, strain, settlement and low-frequency structural vibration are separately specified tasks; they are not inferred automatically from a tilt reading.

faq.q: Which sensors belong in a Smart Infrastructure project?
faq.a: Choose them from the asset’s behaviour and operating risks. Tilt observes local rotation; suitable vibration instrumentation observes dynamic response; radar can measure a validated target distance or water level. Temperature and relevant site records help interpretation. The engineering brief determines the combination, rather than requiring every sensor on every structure.

faq.q: Can the standard machinery vibration sensor monitor a bridge?
faq.a: That cannot be assumed. The published Hitelecom machinery family measures vibration velocity RMS over 10–5,000 Hz. A bridge or tower task may need lower-frequency response, different sensitivity or synchronised waveforms. Confirm the structural measurement objective, instrument and acquisition system separately before specifying the solution.

Monitoring adds observations between inspections and helps focus field work. The responsible engineer still assesses structural condition using appropriate inspections, surveys and other evidence. A configured threshold is a review trigger; it is not an automatic statement of damage, remaining capacity or safe access.

faq.q: Why add temperature or water level to movement monitoring?
faq.a: They answer different questions at the same asset. Temperature can provide context for observed movement; water level can identify a drainage or flooding concern that needs operational attention. Use these channels where relevant to the site, and avoid assuming that correlation proves the cause of structural movement.

faq.q: How are the measurement and reporting intervals selected?
faq.a: Each quantity needs a suitable timescale. A tilt trend, a dynamic vibration record and a rapidly rising sump are different tasks. Agree acquisition, event capture, scheduled reporting, communications delay and available power separately, then confirm how timestamps and delayed or missing records will appear in the platform.

faq.q: Can we include existing surveys and specialist instruments?
faq.a: Yes, as a scoped integration or coordinated review workflow. Define the instrument output, units, timestamp, asset identity and data-access method first. Crack gauges, strain instruments, weather stations and survey records remain separately selected systems; automatic ingestion and analysis depend on the agreed interface and project configuration.

faq.q: What should be added beyond tilt and vibration?
faq.a: Use the asset’s failure modes and exposure to decide. Temperature and wind add loading context; drainage level and water-leak sensors address flooding or equipment ingress. Crack width, strain, settlement and pore-water pressure require dedicated instruments when those quantities matter to the engineer. Select their acquisition and interface explicitly; a generic controller cannot directly read every specialist sensor, and tilt alone does not measure settlement or capacity.
